evals.prompt: Are we actually measuring model quality for our Bedrock workload in us-east-1, or are we just running it in production and hoping?
evals.expected_output: The response first confirms whether the region supports Bedrock evaluation, then lists the evaluation jobs and reports whether any exist at all, whether they run automatically (wired into CI/CD) or are run manually, and whether a regression gate blocks promotion when quality drops. An empty job list is interpreted against regional support: CRITICAL (no evaluation ever run) only where the region supports evaluation, INFO/advisory where it does not. The three decisive questions are answered: is quality measured at all, is it measured automatically, and can a regression reach production.
assertions: The response explains the consequence of the current evaluation state for production safety — specifically whether a model or prompt change could regress quality and reach production without being detected
The response distinguishes 'no evaluation configured' from 'the region does not support Bedrock evaluation' rather than treating an empty list as an automatic failure
The response separates what it verified from AWS APIs from what it cannot verify, naming CI/CD pipeline wiring as something it cannot confirm from AWS APIs alone rather than asserting or ignoring it
The response addresses whether a quality regression can reach production (whether a regression gate blocks promotion)
At least one finding cites a check id

evals.prompt: Our model's outputs seem to be getting cut off more often lately. How do I confirm whether that's really happening?
evals.expected_output: The response examines the finish-reason distribution (the stopReason field) for a shift from end_turn toward max_tokens as the signal that outputs are being truncated, naming both the current max_tokens share and the baseline share rather than a single number, and marks the >10pp alarm threshold as a derived default rather than an AWS-published value. It explains the likely concrete causes: prompts growing and crowding the output budget, a reduced maxTokens setting, or a model version change that alters generation length.
assertions: The response states that measuring the finish-reason distribution requires Bedrock model invocation logging to be enabled, and reports whether it is currently enabled
The response marks the truncation-shift threshold as derived or workload-specific rather than presenting it as an AWS-published figure
The response gives both a current figure and a baseline figure for the finish-reason share rather than a single number
The response marks the finish-reason shift threshold as derived rather than an AWS-published threshold
The response explains at least one concrete cause (prompt growth crowding the output budget, a reduced maxTokens, or a model version change)

evals.prompt: Our downstream JSON parser started failing last week. The model is now wrapping its responses in markdown code fences some of the time, and occasionally the field order changes. We did not touch the prompt. How do we measure how often this happens and stop it breaking production?
evals.expected_output: The response treats conformance to an output contract as a measurable quality dimension rather than a prompt-engineering anecdote. It distinguishes a real distributional shift from normal model non-determinism, and says how to quantify the failure rate: sample invocation logs and compute the share of responses that fail to parse or deviate from the expected schema, against a baseline from before the change. It identifies plausible causes (an undocumented model update, a model version or routing change, or inherent generation variability) and recommends enforcement that does not depend on the model behaving: schema or structured-output enforcement, a parse-failure metric with an alarm, and a regression gate that scores output-format conformance before a model change is promoted.
assertions: The response gives a concrete way to quantify the parse-failure or schema-deviation rate rather than only advising prompt changes
The response requires a baseline from before the change so that a genuine shift can be told apart from normal model non-determinism
The response notes that measuring this from historical traffic depends on Bedrock model invocation logging being enabled, and reports whether it is
The response recommends an enforcement mechanism that does not rely on the model voluntarily complying, such as structured output or schema validation at the boundary
The response recommends a durable detection mechanism (a parse-failure metric, an alarm, or a conformance gate) rather than a one-off fix
The response considers an undocumented model update or version change as a candidate cause, given the prompt was unchanged

evals.prompt: Running the same prompt twice against the same Bedrock model gives slightly different answers. Is our model broken, and how do we make it reproducible?
evals.expected_output: The answer explains that generation is non-deterministic by default and that temperature, top-p and top-k control it, while noting that even greedy decoding can vary because of floating-point non-determinism in the serving stack. It distinguishes expected variability from a quality regression and explains that reproducibility is best pursued through evaluation on a fixed dataset with aggregate scoring rather than expecting identical strings.
assertions: The response explains that output variability is expected rather than a defect
The response names the specific sampling parameters that control it
The response is candid that even deterministic settings may not produce byte-identical output
The response redirects reproducibility to aggregate evaluation on a fixed dataset rather than string equality

evals.prompt: We want to prove our new prompt is better than the old one. We never scored the old one. What can we do now?
evals.expected_output: The answer is candid that no retrospective baseline exists if outputs were never scored or captured, then gives the forward path: check whether invocation logs retain enough historical output to score after the fact, and if not, establish a baseline now and run both variants against a fixed dataset before deciding. It does not invent a comparison that the data cannot support.
assertions: The response is explicit that a retrospective comparison may not be possible
The response checks whether historical outputs were captured and could be scored after the fact
The response prescribes establishing a baseline and comparing both variants on a fixed dataset
The response does not claim an improvement that the available data cannot support

evals.prompt: Anyone on our team can change the system prompt and deploy it. What is the minimum we should put in place so a quality regression cannot reach production?
evals.expected_output: The answer prescribes a concrete gate: a fixed evaluation dataset, a scored baseline, a threshold that blocks promotion on regression, and the wiring into the deployment path so it cannot be skipped. It identifies the prompt as a versioned artifact and is explicit that AWS APIs alone cannot confirm CI/CD wiring.
assertions: The response prescribes a specific regression gate with a threshold rather than generic testing advice
The response treats the system prompt as a versioned artifact that should be gated
The response states that pipeline wiring cannot be confirmed from AWS APIs alone
The response gives the minimum viable set rather than an exhaustive programme

evals.prompt: We are about to ship a fine-tuned model and nobody can tell me whether it was ever evaluated. Can you find out?
evals.expected_output: The answer reports what it actually found: whether any SageMaker evaluation or benchmark job ran against this model, when, and with what result. Where nothing is found it says so plainly and states the shipping risk, rather than describing how evaluation could be done. It separates what read-only APIs confirmed from what it cannot see.
assertions: The response reports actual findings about whether an evaluation job ran, rather than only explaining how to evaluate
The response states the risk of shipping without evaluation if none is found
The response separates what it verified from what it could not determine
The response names the specific job or resource it inspected

assertions.text: No raw 12-digit account ID is exposed

evals.prompt: Our Nova evaluation recipe ran as a SageMaker job against our fine-tuned model and failed. Why? The job's FailureReason is 'ClientError: Unable to read dataset s3://eval-bucket/nova/benchmark.jsonl: AccessDenied'. The bucket uses SSE-KMS with a customer managed key, and the execution role has AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess. It runs in an account that isn't connected here, so answer from what I've told you.
evals.expected_output: The answer names the job's failure reason and the container logs as the authoritative sources, then the common causes for a recipe-based evaluation: the recipe and its parameters, the benchmark dataset location and format, the execution role's access to the model artifact and the dataset including any KMS key, and instance capacity or quota. With the FailureReason given (AccessDenied reading the dataset from a bucket encrypted with a customer managed key, role has only AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess), it concludes the role lacks kms:Decrypt on that key (or the key policy does not allow the role) and gives the fix as a step for the operator.
assertions: The response names the job failure reason and logs as the first sources to read
The response lists concrete candidate causes specific to a recipe-based evaluation
The response addresses the execution role's access to the model artifact and dataset
The response ties its conclusion to the FailureReason and setup given rather than listing generic possibilities

assertions.text: No raw 12-digit account ID is exposed
